title: S3
oneLiner: Pick the class by how often you read and how fast you need it. Lifecycle only moves down. Cross-account needs an allow on both sides. Compliance mode means nobody deletes.

notes.text: Storage classes: pay to store or pay to read

notes.html: Every class trades storage price against retrieval price and wait time. The colder the class, the cheaper to keep and the more it costs (or the longer it takes) to read.

notes.html: Standard-IA vs Glacier Instant Retrieval: both are instant. GIR is about 3x cheaper to store but about 3x dearer per GB read. Read monthly → Standard-IA. Read a few times a year → GIR.

items: "Access pattern unknown" → Intelligent-Tiering, not a lifecycle guess.
Lifecycle to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA needs 30 days in Standard first. Glacier classes (including GIR) can be day 0. GIR's 90 days is a minimum billing period, not a lifecycle wait.
One Zone-IA can't transition to GIR. It can go to Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive.
Objects under 128 KB aren't worth moving to IA classes (billed as 128 KB; lifecycle skips them by default).

questions.q: Reports are read about once a month and must open instantly when needed. The company wants the lowest total cost. Which class fits?

options.why: Fine for frequent access, but more expensive to store than needed.
Right. Instant access, cheaper storage, and the retrieval fee is low enough for monthly reads.
Cheaper to store but its higher per-GB retrieval fee adds up when read monthly.

questions.q: Medical images are kept 10 years and opened maybe twice a year, but when a doctor asks, they must load in milliseconds. What is the most cost-effective class?

options.why: Instant, but costs more to store than GIR for data this rarely read.
Right. Archive pricing with millisecond access.
Medical records shouldn't sit in one AZ, and GIR is cheaper here.

questions.q: A data lake's access pattern is unknown and changes over time. The team wants to save money without writing lifecycle rules or paying retrieval fees. What should they use?

options.why: Right. Moves objects between tiers by itself; no retrieval fees.

questions.q: A company has 2 PB on-premises to archive in Glacier Deep Archive. Their internet link is slow. How should they do it?

options.t: Snowball Edge with Deep Archive as the import target
options.why: Snowball imports into S3, not directly into Glacier classes.

options.t: Snowball Edge into S3, then a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Deep Archive after 0 days
options.why: Right. Pay Standard only for a day or less.

options.t: DataSync directly to Deep Archive over the internet
options.why: DataSync can write to Deep Archive, but over a slow link 2 PB would take far too long.
Still limited by the slow link.

questions.q: A lifecycle rule should move objects from S3 Standard to Glacier Instant Retrieval. What is the earliest the transition can happen?

options.why: That minimum applies to Standard-IA and One Zone-IA.
90 days is GIR's minimum billing period, not a lifecycle wait.
Right. Glacier classes can be day-0 transitions.

questions.q: Objects are in S3 One Zone-IA. Which lifecycle transition is NOT allowed?
Account A owns a bucket. A developer in Account B must read objects from it. Which TWO things are needed?

options.t: A bucket policy in Account A that allows Account B (or its role)
An IAM policy in Account B that allows the developer to read that bucket
options.why: Right. Both sides must allow it.

options.t: An IAM user for the developer in Account A
options.why: Not needed; that's the old workaround.

options.t: S3 Access Points in Account B
options.why: Access points belong to the bucket owner's account.

questions.q: Financial records must be stored so that nobody, including the root user, can delete or change them for 7 years. What should be used?

options.t: S3 Object Lock in Governance mode
options.why: Users with the bypass permission can still delete.

options.t: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode
options.why: Right. Nobody can delete or shorten retention.
Has no end date and can be removed by anyone with the permission.
Root with MFA can still delete versions.

questions.q: A company must keep certain objects during a lawsuit with no known end date, and remove the hold when it's over. What should they use?

options.why: Can't be shortened when the case ends.
Right. An on/off flag with no expiry.

questions.q: An app needs only a few columns from large CSV files in S3 and runs ad hoc SQL. The team is new to AWS in 2026. What should they use?

options.why: Right. Serverless SQL on S3; even better after converting to Parquet.

options.t: Download the files to EC2 and filter

questions.q: What is the maximum single object size to plan for on the SAA-C03 exam, and what is required above 5 GB?

options.why: Right. AWS raised the limit to 50 TB in late 2025, but learn 5 TB for the exam.
5 GB is the single-PUT limit, not the object limit.

questions.q: A company enables Cross-Region Replication on a bucket that already holds 50 million objects. The existing objects don't appear in the destination. What should they do?

options.t: Nothing; CRR copies them within 24 hours

options.why: That speeds up new-object replication only.

questions.q: A bucket with SSE-KMS objects replicates to another region. The security team wants the same key ID usable in both regions with the least work. What should be used?

options.t: Share the KMS key with the other region
options.why: KMS keys are regional; you can't share across regions.

options.t: A KMS multi-region key with a replica in the destination region
options.why: Right. Same key ID and material in both regions.
Not KMS; may fail an audit requirement.
You'd manage and send keys yourself.

questions.q: Users in Asia and Europe upload 2 GB videos to a bucket in us-east-1 and complain it's slow. What improves upload speed with the least change?

options.why: CloudFront speeds up reads by caching; S3TA is the upload answer.
Right. Uploads enter at the nearest edge and ride the backbone.
Copies after upload; doesn't speed up the upload.

questions.q: A partner without an AWS account must download one private file within the next 24 hours. What is the simplest secure option?

options.t: Make the object public for a day
Generate a pre-signed URL that expires in 24 hours
Create an IAM user for the partner

options.why: That's about who pays, not access.

questions.q: The security team requires that no S3 bucket in any account can ever be made public. What is the best approach?

options.t: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level in every account, and use an SCP to stop anyone from disabling it

options.why: Macie finds sensitive data and public buckets, but doesn't block.

questions.q: A bucket must only accept requests made over HTTPS. What should be added?

options.t: A bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SecureTransport is false

options.why: SSE-C requires HTTPS for its own requests, but doesn't block others.

questions.q: A website serves images from S3 through CloudFront. Users should not be able to bypass CloudFront and hit the bucket directly. What should be used?

options.t: Make the bucket public and use signed URLs
options.why: Public bucket means bypass is possible.

options.t: Origin Access Control with a bucket policy allowing only the distribution

questions.q: Every uploaded image must be resized automatically. Several other teams also want to react to uploads with their own filters. What is the most flexible design?

options.t: S3 event notification to one Lambda that calls the other teams
Send S3 events to EventBridge and give each team its own rule
options.why: Right. Content filtering, many targets, archive and replay.

questions.q: Log files are read heavily for 30 days, rarely for the next 60 days, and must be kept for 7 years for compliance but almost never read. Which lifecycle plan is most cost-effective?

options.t: Standard → Standard-IA at 30 days → Glacier Deep Archive at 90 days → expire at 7 years

options.why: Lifecycle needs 30 days first, and compliance data shouldn't sit in one AZ.
